intro: Early modern schools and contemporary artists have reworked ink through contact with new audiences, other kinds of painting and today’s materials.
alt: Three ink-based portraits in strong scarlet color, luminous wet blossoms and enlarged black brush marks with a rose-colored accent.

variants.name: Shanghai School
variants.look: Strong dark accents work against bright scarlet and floral color.
variants.history: The Shanghai School took shape in a growing urban art market in the late Qing. Ren Yi, also called Ren Bonian, worked across figure and bird-and-flower painting.
variants.when: Make a brush painting that can catch attention at a quick glance.
variants.why: Strong wet and dry brush accents can carry the picture even when bright color competes for attention.

source.label: The Met | Ren Yi in the collection

variants.name: Lingnan School
variants.look: Color gathers where moist strokes meet softly edged leaves and blossoms.
variants.history: The Lingnan School developed in southern China in the early 20th century. Gao Jianfu and other artists explored reform through new subjects and a synthesis of brush traditions.
variants.when: Paint a figure or flower with clear contours and soft changes of atmosphere.
variants.why: Wet wash and carefully placed color can distinguish a crisp detail from surrounding air.

source.label: Hong Kong Museum of Art | Chinese painting and calligraphy

variants.name: contemporary Chinese ink
variants.look: A few enlarged ink marks take over the page and meet a sharp modern block of color.
variants.history: Contemporary artists have used ink and its histories across painting, installation, photography and video. Some play with the scale and legibility of a single mark.
variants.when: Keep a familiar brush mark visible while making an unfamiliar composition.
variants.why: An enlarged stroke exposes its texture and can become a subject in its own right.

source.label: The Met | Ink Art: Past as Present in Contemporary China

prompt: Make one wide image composed of three separate equal-width vertical artworks side by side with precise splits at thirds, full bleed with no gutters. Create three distinctly different Chinese ink-based images of the fictional recognizable heroine with glasses and bun and coffee mug.. The attached portrait is just a character reference. Our character is a 30-year-old woman with light ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, black rectangular glasses always visible, tailored charcoal knee-length sheath dress and fitted blazer with an azure pocket square, blue lanyard, little four-color windowpane clip when feasible. She holds a signature white coffee mug. Freeze identity, repeat the subject in every distinct art idiom. Copy no reference card composition or type. No writing, digits, words or labels; no diptych or pastiche. left: Shanghai School-inspired colorful brush painting on paper, rich scarlet and magenta contrasting full dark assertive brush line, urban flower or fruit vendor's setting. center: Lingnan School-inspired ink and pale-color portrait guide, damp wash and unusual edge bleeds, delicate light and realistic blossom background of warm yellow green, intense gaze. right: Contemporary Chinese ink inspired artwork, lively hybrid of enlarged gestural black ink stains across empty white with tiny off-register modern rose color blocks, eye glasses and low-bun silhouette held as graphic forms.
